blocks.text: In the writings of the Prophets there occur three histories or prophecies about locusts that are remarkable above the rest, and which must therefore be explained here. The first concerns the Egyptian locusts, that is, those sent by God into Egypt after the seven most dreadful plagues, by which the obstinacy of Pharaoh could not be broken [Exod. X, 4. ff.]. In this [col. 461] history, in order to understand what is said about the locusts, these three things must be observed. 1. In general, how great a destruction locusts cause to herbs, crops, trees and every produce of the earth. 2. What was peculiar in these locusts. 3. How they were brought into Egypt and carried away out of Egypt. On the first point we would labour in vain if locusts were as well known to us as to the Arabs and Africans, who learn daily how grievous this evil is. When the harvests are already ripe, or upon meadows and pastures, or upon gardens and orchards, a thousand myriads of locusts descend, which, consuming the labour of a whole year in a few hours, impose famine upon the wretched inhabitants. This voracity and gluttony the Arabs express by the words احتنك [iḥtanaka] to gulp down (a word derived from حنك [ḥanak], that is, the jaws); نعص [naʿaṣa] or لعص [laʿaṣa], to devour (Lam and Nun being interchanged); دبش [dabasha], to strip the bark (which, however, they take of the earth and the fields, not of trees, as if the crops and herbs that the locusts consume were the bark of the earth); بشر [bashara], to scrape like a hide, and to make smooth: جرد [jarada], to make bare and to strip of hair: whence also the very name of the locust, جراد [jarād]. Indeed these little creatures gulp down, devour, strip, scrape and make bare whatever is green in the fields. Nor do they harm by their bite alone; they also scorch by their touch. Moreover لعابهم سم ناقع للنبات والشجر لا يقع علي شي منه الا اهلكه [luʿābuhum samm nāqiʿ li-l-nabāt wa-l-shajar lā yaqaʿu ʿalā shayʾ minhu illā ahlakahu] their saliva is a poison so harmful to herbs and trees that whatever it falls upon, it destroys; as one may read in Damir. Yet these things may seem slight, since they often inflict much more damage dead than alive, infecting the air with a foul and poisonous stench, from which a most severe pestilence follows, so that more myriads of men are carried off by such a plague in a few days than by long wars; as will be said in its place. Hence the same Damir says: ليس في الحيوان اكثر افسان [laysa fī al-ḥayawān akthar afsān] There is no animal more destructive. And Muhammad, as they say: الله خلق الف امة منها ستماية في البحر واربعماية في البر وان اول هلاك هذه الامم الجراد واذا اهلك الجراد تتابع هلاك الامم كنظم السلك [Allāh khalaqa alf umma minhā sittumiʾa fī al-baḥr wa-arbaʿumiʾa fī al-barr wa-inna awwal halāk hādhihi al-umam al-jarād wa-idhā halaka al-jarād tatābaʿa halāk al-umam ka-naẓm al-silk] God created a thousand species of animals, [III, 283] six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land. But the first plague of these is the locust; when it destroys, the ruin of the rest follows, like a strung necklace: that is, as the beads strung on a necklace follow one another ^{(1)}.

[III, 284] But in the Egyptian locusts there was something more grievous than usual. For although no plague is more frequent in Egypt, Moses nevertheless says expressly ^{a)} that there had never been locusts like these, nor would there be in the future; whether because they were larger in bulk, like those Indian locusts which Pliny writes, book 9, ch. 3, fill four cubits, and book 10, ch. 29, are three feet in length, their legs and thighs serving as saws when they have dried out; or, as I rather believe, because they surpassed in number whatever swarm of locusts had ever been anywhere in one place, and were more harmful. This is suggested by the words of the Prophet: that they so covered the surface of the earth [col. 462] that no one could see the ground; and that they settled over the whole land of Egypt, whereas locusts usually fly into this or that field, passing over others; and that they consumed every herb, and all the fruit of the trees, and whatever the hail that had gone before had left.
